1.d4 Nf6 2.c4.name: Indian Defence: Normal Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4.strategy: Grabs a larger share of the centre and fights for d5, so that Nc3 and e4 can follow to build a broad pawn centre. Black may answer with solid or sharp set-ups, and the Indian defences invite White to build a big centre in order to undermine it. The cost is the amount of theory White must know against all these defences.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3.name: Indian Defence: Knights Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight, guards d4 and e5 and keeps the c-pawn in reserve until Black shows its set-up. White can still reach a Queen's Gambit or choose a quieter system that does not need c4 at all. It commits less than 2.c4, but Black has a free choice, and Indian set-ups can still arise.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5.name: Trompowsky Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5.background: Named after Octávio Trompowsky (1897–1984), a one-time Brazilian champion who played it in the 1930s and 1940s. Karel Opočenský also played it in the 1930s, and the opening is also known as the Opočenský Opening.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5.strategy: Threatens Bxf6, which would double Black's pawns, and sidesteps the heavy Indian theory that follows 2.c4. The price is an early bishop move before the centre is settled, which can lose time if Black hits the bishop. Black may accept doubled pawns for the bishop pair, or avoid them altogether.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4.name: Indian Defence: Accelerated London System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4.background: The London System is named after the London tournament of 1922, where it appeared seven times. The Irish-American James Mason had been the first master-level player to use it regularly, including at Vienna 1882, London 1883 and New York 1889.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before e3 shuts it in, then builds a solid set-up whatever Black does. The cost is b2: with the bishop gone from c1 nothing guards that pawn, so a queen on b6 can attack it. The set-up is easy to learn but makes little demand on Black, who can develop freely.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nc3.strategy: Controls e4 and d5 and prepares e4, but blocks the c-pawn, so c4 is not possible. White aims for active bishop development instead. Sound, but a minor choice.

1.d4 Nf6 2.g3.name: Indian Defence: Tartakower Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop to pressure d5 and the long diagonal, in a quiet set-up that White completes later. White develops quietly, but without a pawn on c4 yet Black can take space in the centre. Sound but uncommon, and slower than 2.c4 or 2.Nf3.

1.d4 Nf6 2.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens a path for the f1-bishop, aiming for a slow, solid set-up, but it shuts in the bishop on c1 unless that later goes to b2. Black reaches a comfortable game, since the slow plan puts no early pressure on Black's centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c3.strategy: Props up d4 for a quiet system of piece development, but takes c3 from the queen's knight, and c4 now costs a second tempo. Sound, though Black has a free hand to choose its set-up and White does little to fight for e4 and d5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.b3.name: Basque Opening
1.d4 Nf6 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, but with the pawn already on d4 the bishop mainly supports that pawn until the centre opens. White does little in the centre meanwhile, so Black can take space there or strike at d4. Sound but slow.

1.d4 Nf6 2.d5.name: Indian Defence: Pawn Push Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.d5.strategy: Grabs space and stops ...d5, but moves the d-pawn a second time and makes it a target. Black undermines it with ...e6, and after dxe6 fxe6 White has no advanced central pawn left.

1.d4 Nf6 2.e4.strategy: Offers the e-pawn: 2...Nxe4 wins it, and White must look for compensation in quick development. After 3.Nc3 Nxc3 4.bxc3 White has doubled c-pawns as well as a pawn less.

1.d4 Nf6 2.f3.name: Paleface Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.f3.background: The name Paleface Attack appears in Eric Schiller's 1986 book on the Blackmar–Diemer Gambit, which White usually hopes to reach with e4 and Nc3.
1.d4 Nf6 2.f3.strategy: Prepares e4, but takes f3 from the g1-knight and weakens the kingside, including the e1–h4 diagonal. After 2...d5 3.e4 dxe4 4.fxe4 Nxe4 Black is simply a pawn up, so White usually has to give the pawn for quick development instead.

1.d4 Nf6 2.f4.name: Canard Opening
1.d4 Nf6 2.f4.strategy: Controls e5 and aims for a solid wall of pawns in the centre, but spends a move on the f-pawn that develops nothing and weakens e3, e4 and the e1–h4 diagonal. Black develops freely, and the knight on f6 already watches e4, the hole such a set-up leaves.

1.d4 Nf6 2.g4.name: Indian Defence: Gibbins–Weidenhagen Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.g4.strategy: Offers the g-pawn: after 2...Nxg4, e3 or e4 opens the queen's diagonal to the knight on g4. Black keeps the extra pawn by guarding the knight or retreating it, and White's kingside stays weakened for little in return.

1.d4 Nf6 2.b4.strategy: Gains queenside space and prepares Bb2, but leaves the b-pawn loose: after ...e6 the f8-bishop threatens ...Bxb4+, so White must spend a move defending the pawn or give it up. It develops nothing and weakens the queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.a3.strategy: A waiting move that stops ...Bb4+ and prepares b4, but it develops nothing and fights for no central square. Black gains time to build the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.a4.strategy: Controls b5 and gains a little queenside space, but it develops nothing and weakens b4. Black builds the centre while White still has most of the army to develop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.h3.strategy: Stops ...Ng4 and a later ...Bg4, but it spends a tempo on a rim pawn that neither develops a piece nor adds to the centre. Black takes space in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.h4.strategy: Starts a rim-pawn advance with ideas of Bg5 and h5, but develops nothing and weakens g4 and the kingside. Black takes the centre at leisure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nd2.strategy: Blocks the bishop on c1 and takes the queen's guard from d4, so ...c5 or ...e5 hits an unprotected pawn. The knight eyes e4 and c4, but the clumsy set-up costs time that Black uses in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Na3.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes c4 and b5 but guards neither d4 nor e4. White loses time while Black builds the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nh3.strategy: Heads for f4 via the rim, but on f4 the knight can be chased by ...e5 or ...g5, and until then it does nothing for the centre. Black builds the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bd2.strategy: Develops the bishop on a passive square where it takes d2 from the queen's knight and blocks the queen's guard of d4. Developing the same bishop actively outside the pawn chain would keep d2 and the d-file open.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Be3.strategy: Develops the bishop in front of the e-pawn, so the f1-bishop stays shut in. ...Ng4 hits it at once and wins a tempo: White must retreat the bishop or give it up for the knight, doubling its e-pawns after fxe3.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Qd2.strategy: Brings the queen out too early, where it shuts in the bishop on c1, takes d2 from the knight and aims at nothing. Black develops freely.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Qd3.strategy: Develops the queen before any minor piece, blocking d3 for the f1-bishop. Black can harass it with natural developing moves, and White still has the whole army to bring out.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Kd2.strategy: Gives up castling and shuts in the queen and bishop. 2...Ne4+ forces the king to move again at once, and it has no safe home in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bh6.strategy: Loses the bishop for nothing: 2...gxh6 takes it with a pawn. Black's h-pawns are doubled and isolated, but a whole piece is far more than that is worth.

1.d4 Nf6.name: Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6.background: The earliest known use of the term “Indian Defence” dates from 1884, attributed to the openings played by the Indian player Moheschunder Bannerjee against John Cochrane, and Savielly Tartakower popularised it in the early 1920s. Championed by the hypermodern school in the 1920s, these defences were fully accepted only after Russian players showed in the late 1940s that they are sound for Black.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6.strategy: Opens the diagonal for the king's bishop and keeps Black's set-up flexible: Black can pin a knight, fianchetto the queen's bishop or challenge the centre at once, and chooses only after seeing White's third move. The price is the c8-bishop, which the e6-pawn shuts in, so it usually comes out via a fianchetto.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and castle, and lets White build a broad pawn centre that Black then attacks from the flank. The positions are sharp and unbalanced, usually with play on opposite wings, and both sides play for a win. The price is White's extra space and a large body of theory.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once and aims for a queenside pawn majority, backed by a fianchettoed king's bishop. Black gives White space and a strong pawn on d5 in return, so Black must find active play before the cramp tells. The games are unbalanced and often sharp.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 with a compact set-up and keeps the choice between a solid bishop on e7 and a King's Indian fianchetto open. It is solid but usually cramped, because the bishop on e7 is less active than one on g7, and it lacks the dynamic chances of the King's Indian.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and presses on d4 so that ...e5 can follow, hoping to induce White to push its pawns too early. The knight blocks the c-pawn, and a developing reply discourages ...e5, so Black often switches to a more modest set-up. Sound but offbeat, and highly transpositional.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c6.name: Slav Indian
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 and a solid pawn chain, with the c8-bishop still free to come out before the e-pawn shuts it in. The c-pawn is committed early, so a quick ...c5 would cost a tempo, but Black can still build a compact pawn centre instead.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 b6.name: Accelerated Queen's Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 b6.background: It is considered less accurate than the standard Queen's Indian move order 2...e6 3.Nf3 b6: in Alekhine–König, Vienna 1922, White was better after 3.Nc3 Bb7 4.Qc2 d5 5.cxd5 Nxd5 6.Nf3. James Plaskett and Raymond Keene analyse the line in their 1987 book on the English Defence.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to control e4 and d5. Until the e-pawn moves, the f8-bishop cannot pin a knight on c3, so White can develop and prepare e4 freely; stopping that with ...d5 lets White gain time against the knight after the exchange on d5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5.strategy: Sacrifices a pawn for quick development and active piece play, and usually wins it back. White can try to keep the extra pawn or return it for a lead in development, so the game turns on whether Black's activity outweighs the material. Rarely played at grandmaster level.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once, but White simply takes it: after 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.Nf3, White gains time against the knight and builds a broad centre without allowing the counter ...e5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 b5.name: Indian Defence: Pyrenees Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn for queenside pressure, but without a pawn on d5 and without ...c5 to open the queenside. After 3.cxb5 White is a clean pawn ahead, and the pressure along the queenside does not make up for it while White develops in peace.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 and keeps White's pieces off b5, but does nothing for the centre or development. Black spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move while White builds the centre at leisure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 a5.strategy: Stops b4 but contributes nothing to development or the fight for the centre. A tempo is spent on the rook's pawn while White occupies the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 and can recapture on c5 if Black strikes there with the c-pawn. From a6 it does nothing for d5 or e5, and White takes an easy central edge.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 h6.strategy: Prevents Bg5 but spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move and leaves the centre alone. White simply builds the centre and has a lead in development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rook's pawn and does nothing for the centre or development; with the pawn past h6, Black can no longer meet Bg5 with ...h6. White develops freely, builds the centre and has a clear lead in development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Ng8.strategy: Undoes the knight's development and costs two tempi. White has a full centre and the move, and Black has to start again with ...Nf6.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Ng4.strategy: Moves the same knight a second time without a target: f2 and h2 are both guarded, and h3 can drive it back later. White builds the centre and gains further time against the knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nh5.strategy: Moves the knight a second time, to the rim, where its only forward squares, f4 and g3, are covered by White. White takes the centre and is clearly ahead in development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Ne4.strategy: Moves the knight again to e4, where Qc2 or f3 chase it with a gain of time. Black has no pawn on d5 or f5 yet to support it, and White builds a broad centre with the time gained.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Rg8.strategy: Wastes a tempo with the rook and forfeits the right to castle kingside for good, while the centre and development are untouched.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g5.name: Indian Defence: Medusa Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g5.strategy: Loses a pawn at once: 3.Bxg5 wins it, and after 3...Ne4 the bishop simply retreats while the weakened kingside leaves Black no real compensation.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 Nd5.strategy: Hangs the knight: 3.cxd5 wins it for nothing, because the d7-pawn blocks the queen's defence of d5 and no other piece guards the square.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e6.strategy: Opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop and keeps both a solid central set-up and a fianchetto of the c8-bishop in reach. Black stays flexible and sound. The price is a c8-bishop hemmed in by the e6-pawn, which usually has to find its diagonal by a fianchetto.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and kingside castling, and keeps both a King's Indian and a Grünfeld set-up open. Black lets White build a centre first and plans to strike at it later with pawn breaks. The cost is that White has the first say in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Meets the pawn with a pawn and takes a share of the centre, which also lets the c8-bishop come out before ...e6. The game heads for classical queen's pawn structures. The cost is that White decides which structure arises.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to bear on e4 and the long diagonal, and keeps a solid pawn set-up in hand. Black controls the centre from a distance rather than occupying it. The cost is that the centre stays with White for now.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and heads for a Benoni-type structure, trading central space for queenside counterplay. It is less common than the main replies, and White, not obliged to play c4, can build a big centre and press with extra space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d6.name: Indian Defence: Tartakower Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: Frees the c8-bishop and prepares to challenge the centre later, while several set-ups stay open. Sound but modest: the d6-pawn claims less space than ...d5, and White keeps a free choice of set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 behind a solid pawn chain and keeps other set-ups in reserve. White need not play c4, and the c6-pawn has taken the natural square of the b8-knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Ne4.name: Döry Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Ne4.background: The Döry Defence was the subject of a theme tournament in Vienna in 1937, won by Paul Keres. It is uncommon, and sometimes transposes into a variation of the Queen's Indian Defence.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Ne4.strategy: Puts the knight on a central post at once, to be supported later by pawn moves or a fianchetto of the c8-bishop. This knight has now moved twice, and White can challenge it with a knight to d2, aiming to trade it off or, after Nfd2, to drive it back with f3 and gain time for e4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight but invites 3.d5, which attacks it at once. 3...Ne5 loses the piece to 4.Nxe5, so the knight goes back to b8 or to a5 or b4, where it is soon driven on, and White has gained space and time.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does nothing for the centre. White can take space in the centre while the piece stays out of play.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Rg8.strategy: Moves the rook for no purpose, wasting a tempo and giving up the right to castle kingside. No other piece is developed and the king has lost its natural shelter.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 a6.name: Indian Defence: Knights Variation, Alburt-Miles Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: Prepares to expand on the queenside but spends a tempo on a rim pawn while the centre and development are untouched. White can build the centre at leisure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: Stops b4 and gains queenside space, but spends a tempo on a rim pawn and leaves the b5-square weak. Neither the centre nor development is addressed, so White simply builds the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 b5.name: Indian Defence: Polish Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Grabs queenside space and prepares ...Bb7, but spends a tempo on a pawn push with only one piece developed. The b5-pawn becomes a target: e3 or e4 opens the f1-bishop's diagonal to it, and a4 or c4 attack it as well.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: Stops Bg5 for the price of a tempo and does nothing for the centre or development. White builds the centre as if Black had passed, and the kingside pawns are loosened.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Weakens g5 and g6 without developing anything. White takes the free tempo to build the centre, and the advanced h-pawn gains nothing in return.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Ng8.strategy: Retreats the knight to where it began, undoing Black's first move. White gets two free tempi in the centre and can set up as it likes.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Ng4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time with no real threat, since the f3-knight and the h1-rook guard h2 and the king guards f2. 3.h3 drives it back, so Black has lost a tempo while White gains a useful move.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Nh5.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, from where 3.g4 drives it back with gain of space; 3...Nf4 would lose it to 4.Bxf4. Black has spent two moves on the knight and developed nothing else.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 Nd5.strategy: Centralises the knight, but 3.c4 or 3.e4 drives it away with tempo, so that it moves a third time while White builds a broad pawn centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 e5.strategy: Loses a pawn for little: the f3-knight and the d4-pawn both attack e5, and after 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 White is simply a pawn up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn, which both Nf3 and Bc1 attack and nothing defends, so 3.Bxg5 or 3.Nxg5 wins a pawn for nothing and leaves Black's kingside loosened.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 Ne4.strategy: Attacks the bishop at once, so White must move it again or defend it; Black gives up a tempo of development for that. Black then keeps the knight on e4 and strikes at the centre, and if White chases it with f3, that pawn takes the best square from White's own knight. The careless 3.Nf3 allows 3...Nxg5 4.Nxg5 e5, and the discovered attack on the knight regains the lost time.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 e6.strategy: Lets the queen recapture if White takes on f6, so Black avoids doubled pawns, and opens the diagonal of the f8-bishop. The price is a pinned knight, and White can build a broad centre at once. If White does take on f6, Black keeps the bishop pair and an intact pawn structure against White's centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 d5.background: Magnus Carlsen chose the Trompowsky, an uncommon opening at the elite level, in the first game of the 2016 World Chess Championship, and Sergey Karjakin answered 2...d5. After 3.e3 c5 4.Bxf6 gxf6 the game was drawn in 42 moves.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 d5.strategy: Takes the centre at once and allows Bxf6, doubling Black's pawns. Black usually recaptures with the e-pawn, keeping a defensible structure and opening diagonals for the queen and the f8-bishop, though recapturing with the g-pawn is also common. In return Black has the bishop pair, and White has spent two moves on a bishop only to trade it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 and plans to trade the c-pawn for White's d-pawn. With the bishop gone from c1, ...Qb6 hits b2, so White must defend it or offer the pawn. White can also take on f6 first; once its pawns are doubled, Black relies on the bishop pair and play against White's centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop. It is sound, but 3.Bxf6 forces 3...exf6, away from the centre, and the doubled f-pawns block the fianchettoed bishop in return for the bishop pair.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 c6.background: In Djordjević–Kovačević, Bela Crkva 1984, White played 3.e3?? and resigned after 3...Qa5+ in view of 4...Qxg5. Graham Burgess, in The Quickest Chess Victories of All Time, calls it “the shortest ever loss by a master”.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 c6.strategy: Opens the d8-a5 diagonal and prepares ...Qb6 against the b2-pawn, unguarded since the bishop left c1. White must avoid 3.e3??, because 3...Qa5+ attacks king and bishop at once; several other replies are sound. An offbeat but sound move.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4 but blocks the c-pawn, so the ...c5 break has to wait. 3.d5 drives the knight to e5, where it can be chased again, and 3.Bxf6 doubles Black's pawns at once. Sound, but slower than the central replies.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop. After 3.Bxf6 exf6 Black has doubled f-pawns, and White can build a broad centre at leisure. Playable, but slower than the central replies.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 d6.strategy: Opens the c8-bishop and prepares a flexible set-up, but leaves the centre to White for now. After 3.Bxf6 exf6 White can take the broader pawn centre, and Black has the bishop pair for the doubled f-pawns. Sound, but more passive than the central replies.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 h6.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop at once instead of developing. 3.Bxf6 exf6 doubles Black's pawns and leaves ...h6 a lost tempo, while 3.Bh4 g5 4.Bg3 loosens Black's kingside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it contests neither d4 nor e5, and does nothing against 3.Bxf6. White develops freely.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 a6.strategy: A rim-pawn move that develops nothing and does nothing against Bxf6. White builds up at leisure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 a5.strategy: Gains a little queenside space but develops nothing and does nothing against Bxf6, which doubles Black's pawns. White gets its development for free.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 b5.strategy: Advances the b-pawn before a second piece is developed and weakens c6 and the queenside. The pawn is already a target: 3.Qd3 or 3.a4 hits it, and Black must spend another move on it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 h5.strategy: A flank pawn move that develops nothing and weakens g5 and g6 for good. It does not stop 3.Bxf6, which doubles Black's pawns while White develops.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 Ng8.strategy: Returns the knight to its starting square and undoes Black's only developing move. White has d4 and the active bishop on g5 for free and a clear lead in development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 Ng4.strategy: Moves the knight again without creating a threat, to a square where 3.h3 hits it at once. Then 3...Nf6 has only lost time, and 3...Nh6 4.Bxh6 gxh6 wrecks Black's kingside pawns.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 Nh5.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where 3.e3 or 3.e4 opens the queen's diagonal and threatens Qxh5. Black must then guard it with ...g6, leaving it offside, or bring it back to f6 with two tempi lost.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 Nd5.strategy: Centralises the knight, but on d5 it is a target: 3.c4 or 3.e4 attacks it at once. White gains central space with tempo while Black has moved the same piece twice.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 Rg8.strategy: Gives up kingside castling for good and spends a tempo guarding g7, which the f8-bishop already guards. White develops freely, and Bxf6 still doubles Black's pawns.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bg5 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn, but after 3.dxe5 the knight is pinned to the queen, since e7 is now empty: 3...Ne4 or 3...Ng4 allows 4.Bxd8. Black stays at least a pawn down.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 d5.name: London System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 d5.strategy: Meets the pawn with a pawn and builds the classical centre, with the c8-bishop free to come out. White gets the set-up it wants, a solid pawn chain and a knight heading for e5, and Black gets a sound game in which White has the clearer plans. The cost is that e5 is hard to contest: the f4-bishop and the d4-pawn make it a fine outpost.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 e6.strategy: Opens the diagonal of the f8-bishop and keeps every set-up open: a central pawn stand, a fianchetto of the queen's bishop, or a break against d4. It also guards d5 and f5 against White's pieces. The cost is a c8-bishop shut in behind the e6-pawn, which needs a plan to come into play.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 c5.background: An early ...c5 is described as a popular response to the London System at higher levels of play. Johnsen and Kovačević considered 1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 c5 3.e3 Qb6 the most critical line.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 c5.strategy: Challenges d4 at once and aims at the b2-pawn, which no bishop guards any more: after 3.e3 the reply 3...Qb6 hits it, and White must defend it or offer it for activity. White's other way is to gain space in the centre. The price is a sharper game in which Black's development can lag if the queen sortie comes to nothing.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and castle short, a set-up that exerts its pressure from a distance. Black leaves the centre to White for now and must prepare a break against it. Against this set-up White does better with the bishop on e2 than on d3, where the fianchettoed bishop leaves it little scope.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, where it controls e4. It is sound, but it does not challenge d4 and commits the b-pawn before Black knows White's plan, while White develops freely. The same set-up is available after ...e6, which keeps a central pawn stand and a break against d4 in hand as well.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 d6.strategy: Frees the c8-bishop and prepares ...e5 against the f4-bishop or a fianchetto of the king's bishop. It is sound but modest: the d6-pawn claims less space than ...d5, and White develops comfortably or takes space in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a solid structure in which the c8-bishop can come out to f5, and opens the d8-b6 diagonal for ...Qb6 against b2. It is sound but less direct than ...c5: the pawn takes c6 from the b8-knight, and ...c5 later costs a second tempo.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 Ne4.strategy: Puts the knight on a central post at once, to be supported later by ...d5. White can challenge it or drive it back with a pawn, so Black has spent two moves on one piece. Sound enough, but not recommended: White develops comfortably while the knight looks for a role.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 Nh5.strategy: Attacks the bishop and aims for ...Nxf4, which would give Black the bishop pair. White can keep the bishop by moving it, after which e3 opens the d1-h5 diagonal so that the knight on the rim must move again, or allow the trade and recapture for control of e5. Sound enough, but Black spends time on the knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight but blocks the c-pawn and allows 3.d5, which attacks it at once. The knight cannot go to e5, where Bxe5 wins it, so it must retreat, and White gains space with tempo.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 Na6.strategy: Sends the knight to the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 and guards c7 but does nothing for the centre. White develops freely or takes more space with c4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 Rg8.strategy: Gives up kingside castling for good, and its only point, a later ...g5 against the bishop, loosens Black's position further. White simply develops while Black's king stays in the centre or must castle long.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move that neither develops a piece nor fights for the centre. White develops at leisure, or takes space in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rook's pawn: it takes b4 away but develops nothing, leaves b5 weak and does not fight for the centre. White develops at leisure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 b5.strategy: Gains queenside space and prepares ...Bb7, but weakens c6 and leaves the b5-pawn without support: e3 opens the f1-bishop's diagonal to it, and a4 or Nc3 attack it as well. Black must spend further time on the pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn as a gambit, aiming for ...Ng4 and ...Nc6 against e5. After 3.dxe5 the f4-bishop already guards the pawn and a knight on f3 adds a second guard, so Black struggles to win it back and has limited counterplay.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 h6.strategy: Takes g5 away and prepares ...g5 to drive the bishop back, but it delays development and loosens the kingside. After ...g5 the bishop retreats to g3 and stays on a good diagonal.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 h5.strategy: Advances the rook's pawn to support a knight on g4, but develops nothing and weakens g5 and the kingside. White develops and faces no threat.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 Ng8.strategy: Returns the knight to g8 and wastes the first move, so White has played d4 and Bf4 against an undeveloped army and can take the centre at will.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 Ng4.strategy: Moves the knight again to a square where it hits f2 and h2, but both are guarded, and 3.h3 drives it back with gain of time. Black has developed nothing else.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 Nd5.strategy: Attacks the unprotected bishop, but White keeps it with 3.Bg3 and then threatens c4 or e4 to drive the knight back with gain of time. Black has moved the same knight twice and is behind in development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Bf4 g5.strategy: Attacks the bishop, but the pawn on g5 is unprotected: 3.Bxg5 wins it at once, and after ...Rg8 White can trade on f6 and keep the extra pawn. Black's kingside is loosened for nothing.

1.d4 Nf6 2.f3 d5.strategy: The principled reply: the pawn takes control of e4, so White's planned central push becomes a gambit, and it punishes the f-pawn's advance, which takes the natural square from the king's knight. Black takes the centre and can develop calmly.

1.d4 Nf6 2.g4 Nxg4.strategy: Takes the pawn and puts the knight on g4, where it eyes h2 and f2. Black wins material and White pays with a lead in development and the chance of a broad centre, so Black has to hand time back and keep the position solid.

1.d4 Nf6 2.g4 e5.strategy: Ignores the pawn and strikes at the centre at once. If White takes on e5, the knight can capture on g4 and attack the pawn that took, but Black opens the centre before developing, a sharper and riskier way to meet the gambit.
1.d4 Nf6 2.g4 e5.name: Indian Defence: Gibbins-Weidenhagen Gambit, Oshima Defence

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Takes a share of the centre and stops the e-pawn from advancing, which is what White's knight move prepares. The knight on c3 also blocks the c-pawn, so White cannot build the usual queen's-pawn pressure and the game stays flexible and quiet.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: A pawn sacrifice: White takes with tempo on the knight, which goes to g4 and eyes the pawn on e5. White can hold the extra pawn by developing the bishop to f4, and Black has little to show for the risk.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nc3 e5.name: Indian Defence: Maddigan Gambit

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5.strategy: Challenges the centre from the side, but with the knight on c3 White can play e4 at once and gets more space than in the usual structure. Taking on d5 later is a trap for Black: after e4 and ...exd5, e5 kicks the knight away and leaves White clearly better.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nc3 c5.name: Indian Defence: Reversed Chigorin Defence

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nd2 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn in the hope of a trap with the knight on g4. The gambit is considered unsound, so Black is a pawn down for quick piece play, which works only against a careless White.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nd2 e5.name: Indian Defence: Lazard Gambit
